metadata.title: JZ Mock D · Paper 1
metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and reviewed follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: Both choose terms from repeated multi-term brackets so their total exponents meet the target, then count the different contributing selections. The mock collects several selections for one x-power; the candidate requires fixed counts of x and y² simultaneously.

Both filter algebraically obtained trigonometric levels and count all angle branches on a specified interval, including endpoint restrictions. The candidate practises the branch-counting stage with cosine and an expanded triple-angle interval; it does not practise the mock’s tangent-modulus sign quadratics.

Both determine the attainable range of an inner function, complete the outer quadratic square and compare only its permitted vertex/endpoints. The mock must prove the modulus-distance lower bound; the candidate reads a finite inner range from the graph and asks its output spread.
Both differentiate fractional-power expressions, factor out a power with known sign on the domain, locate the derivative’s negative interval and calculate its length.

Both use factored derivative sign tables to identify monotonicity intervals. The candidate adds a second function and intersects opposite-sign cases rather than measuring the length of one function’s decreasing interval.

The candidate practises the prerequisite of replacing coordinate moduli by straight-line branches, constructing one diamond and finding its area. The mock additionally requires the decisive intersection of two translated regions and finding the new common polygon; the candidate does not reproduce that intersection step.

Both express an AP block sum through its term count and symmetric midpoint term. The candidate cancels two partial sums to isolate a three-term block; the mock separates odd/even subsequences with unequal counts and compares their total and difference.

Both simplify a quotient containing a sum of square roots by the difference-of-squares factorisation before doing the next operation. The candidate then integrates the simplified rate; it practises the surd-cancellation prerequisite, not the mock’s neighbour-by-neighbour finite-sum cancellation.

Both extract circle centres/radii, find the centre separation and use an attained radial configuration for an extremal point distance. The candidate asks the greatest distance; the mock asks the least and must first recognise intersecting circles, so a radius-subtraction rule is not transferred blindly.

Both obtain circle centres/radii and compare their separation with the radii before finding the minimum distance between the circumferences. The candidate is externally disjoint; the mock’s intersecting configuration produces a different minimum-distance case.
Both use an exponential of a trigonometric expression as one variable, retain its exact attained interval and optimise the resulting quadratic by its vertex and endpoints.

Both substitute a positive exponential variable and optimise a quadratic on its attainable range. The candidate then reverses the optimisation for a positive reciprocal; the mock has a bounded trigonometric inner range and no reciprocal.

Both use stated polynomial factors to impose exact conditions on unknown coefficients. The candidate evaluates at two linear-factor roots and solves their equations; the mock uses a given quadratic factor to build a quotient and compare coefficients. Divisibility-to-coefficient constraints are the shared prerequisite, with the quotient calculation additional in the mock.

Both use cubic turning-point heights and branch monotonicity to justify how many distinct real intersections occur, with strict boundary cases. The candidate determines a horizontal-level parameter interval; the mock applies its known three-root configuration to transformed equations.

Both rotate a parabola a quarter-turn about a non-origin centre by translating to relative coordinates, rotating and translating back. Vertex/orientation tracking checks the full transformed equation. The mock composes two rotations and solves for the second centre.
Both apply an off-axis horizontal reflection and input translation to a sine/cosine graph in order, tracking extrema and phase. The mock adds horizontal scaling and vertical-line reflections.

Both execute a sequence of graph translations, reflections and horizontal scaling using input/output substitutions in the stated order. The candidate then expands a quadratic; the mock additionally reduces a trigonometric phase after two vertical-line reflections.

Both identify the geometric ratio of a trigonometric series, check convergence and replace the series by its exact sum. The candidate evaluates a numerical signed GP; the mock’s ratio depends on the angle and the summed expression must then be solved with the original domains retained.

Both calculate point-to-circle-centre distance from squared coordinate differences. The candidate isolates which data determine that distance; the mock must first construct the incircle centre/radius from tangency and compare the distance with the radius. Only the squared-distance prerequisite is shared.

Both identify the original input intervals represented by a transformed-function integral and combine signed interval contributions. The candidate uses input translation and linear combinations; the mock adds horizontal compression, complete-period counting and an arithmetic sum.

Both divide a definite integral at the change points of a case-defined function and add the appropriate signed pieces. The candidate uses modulus branches and polynomial antiderivatives; the mock uses floor-defined constant strips, logarithmic combination and reversed limits.

Both analyse a modulus recurrence on suitable input regions, prove its repeated behaviour at a distant index and integrate the resulting piecewise function. The update rule and sign/interval partition differ, so the candidate cannot be solved by copying the mock’s final triangular graph.

Both express several data conditions through a GP first term and ratio, eliminate those parameters and evaluate another quantity. The candidate uses infinite sums of powered terms and convergence; the mock uses four finite terms, reciprocal sums and a product identity.

lessons.title: Combine logarithms before solving

lessons.title: Find the inner range first

Use equal averages of symmetric AP terms and arithmetic sum formulae.

lessons.title: Read the ratio before summing

lessons.title: Move the input and the height

Interpret translations, stretches and reflections through their effect on input and output.

lessons.title: Read a circle from its equation
knowledge: Complete squares in both coordinates to read a circle centre and radius.
Find a circle from diameter endpoints using midpoint and distance.
Distinguish a positive-radius circle, a single point and no real circle from the squared radius.

lessons.title: Read the input scale of a trig graph

Use sin²x+cos²x=1 to reduce an equation to one trigonometric function.

lessons.title: Rewrite powers before differentiating
knowledge: Rewrite quotients, roots and products as sums of powers before differentiating.
Apply the power rule to rational exponents on the appropriate domain.

lessons.title: Read the shape from derivative signs
knowledge: Factor the derivative and test its sign between zeros and domain breaks.
Use derivative sign changes to classify local maxima and minima.
A zero derivative without a sign change need not be a local extreme.
Use the original function to find stationary-point heights.

lessons.title: Integrate powers, then use the missing information

Include an integration constant and determine it from an initial value on the same interval; an excluded point can separate intervals with different constants.
Evaluate a definite integral as an antiderivative at the upper limit minus its value at the lower limit.

lessons.title: Separate signed accumulation from total area
knowledge: Distinguish a signed integral from total geometric area.
Find all intersections and integrate upper minus lower on each separate region.
Split when a curve crosses or an absolute-value formula changes.

lessons.title: Simplify lengths before finding an area
knowledge: Simplify square-root lengths using sqrt(z²)=|z| and the sign supplied by the geometric domain.

lessons.title: Keep every factor in a binomial coefficient

Transform the whole input interval and count endpoint solutions carefully.
State the tangent domain and multiply by a denominator only within that domain.

lessons.title: Find the allowed range before optimising

lessons.title: Use centres and list the geometry cases
knowledge: Use centre distance and radii to find greatest separation between two circles.
For an unspecified right angle, examine each possible triangle vertex.
Use negative reciprocal gradients for nonvertical perpendicular lines and handle vertical/horizontal lines directly.
Use a quadratic root sum when only the sum is needed, while rejecting degeneracy and duplicates.

lessons.title: Turn distance into a quadratic
knowledge: Choose the actual optimisation objective, distinguishing height from distance.
Minimise squared distance using both coordinates of the moving point.
Keep the nonnegative range of a squared substitution when minimising the resulting quadratic.
Convert modulus bounds to intervals and check that proposed product extremes can occur together.

lessons.title: Count roots from the turning heights

Evaluate turning heights on the original function to count axis crossings or intersections with a horizontal level.

lessons.title: Move the graph and keep the signed area

Reflecting in y=k sends a height y to 2k−y.

lessons.title: Simplify surds and rationalise
knowledge: Extract square factors and combine like surds.
Multiply by a nonzero conjugate to rationalise a denominator.

Keep sqrt(x²)=|x| and all original denominator exclusions.

lessons.title: Divide polynomials and use remainders
knowledge: Divide polynomials by cancelling the highest power, multiplying back and subtracting the full product.
Stop when the remainder degree is lower than the divisor degree.
Evaluate a polynomial at a linear divisor’s zero to find a remainder or test a factor.
Subtract remainder equations to remove unneeded coefficients.

lessons.title: Circle angles, chords and tangents
knowledge: Add the radius at a tangent or the perpendicular from centre to chord to obtain a right triangle.
Apply centre/circumference, semicircle, same-segment, cyclic-quadrilateral and alternate-segment angle results to the correct chord or arc.
Separate internal and external circle-contact cases using centre distance and radii.
Use a right triangle for an internal common tangent of equal circles.

lessons.title: Vectors and transformations
knowledge: Calculate a displacement vector by subtracting start from finish and combine components.
Use related vectors to establish parallelism or collinearity.
Transform displacement relative to the stated centre for rotations and enlargements.
Apply transformations in order and distinguish length, area and volume scale factors, including negative enlargement factors.

lessons.title: Test NECESSARY and SUFFICIENT separately
knowledge: Keep the target fixed: sufficiency tests condition implies target, while necessity tests target implies condition.
Classify a condition by proving each successful direction and giving an allowed counterexample for each failed direction.
Necessary and sufficient describes both directions, as in an if-and-only-if condition.
A stronger condition may be sufficient without being necessary.
For ax+by=c with nonzero coefficients, gradient and intercept signs are determined by -a/b and c/b.

lessons.title: Observe a cycle, then prove the rule repeats it
knowledge: Initial terms suggest a cycle; the recurrence must establish return to the same state.
When a recurrence depends on the index, the index phase must also repeat.
Find a distant term from its position within a proved repeating block.
Compute a long sum using complete blocks and leftover terms.
Repeating terms need not give repeating partial sums when a whole block has nonzero sum; a finite list without a rule does not force its continuation.

lessons.title: Collect all contributions to a coefficient
knowledge: To find a coefficient in a product, list every pair of exponents whose sum is the target exponent.
Multiply the matching coefficients and add all contributions.
The coefficient of x^k in (1+x)^n is the binomial coefficient n choose k.
Substituting x=1 sums all coefficients; it gives one target coefficient only when the contributing terms exhaust that whole row.
For a constant term with positive and negative powers, require the total exponent to be zero.

lessons.title: Use an identity at useful inputs
knowledge: An identity holds at every allowed input; useful substitutions can make function arguments coincide or produce simultaneous equations.
Opposite heights equally spaced around a centre imply a zero value at that centre and signed integral cancellation on intervals with that midpoint.
Symmetry about one centre does not guarantee cancellation on an interval with a different midpoint.
Write the transformed input for each graph operation, then compare the two operation orders.
An identity f(x+T)=f(x) establishes a period, not necessarily the smallest positive period; positive integer multiples are also periods.
Replacing x by -x reflects roots and exchanges their positive and negative signs.

lessons.title: Find the full parameter range
knowledge: Check parameter values at which an equation changes degree before using a quadratic discriminant or dividing by a coefficient.
A nondegenerate quadratic has two distinct real roots for positive discriminant and one distinct repeated root for zero discriminant.
The substitution u=x^2 retains u>=0: positive u gives two real x values, zero gives one and negative u gives none.
Two distinct positive roots of the quadratic in u are needed for four distinct real roots of an even quartic; use discriminant, root sum and product.
Use cubic turning heights to classify real-root counts and inspect zero turning heights at parameter boundaries.
Prove the full necessary-and-sufficient range; a narrower sufficient condition alone does not describe all successful parameters.

lessons.title: Prove a bound and attain it
knowledge: An extremal solution requires a bound excluding every better value and a construction attaining that bound.
Round a lower bound on an integer count upward, then check that the proposed arrangement works.
Circular chair coverage requires checking the wrap-around gap as well as internal gaps.
Sort data to use medians, range and mean constraints; bound the total in terms of the median and then build an attaining list.
For a sorted triple with mean mu and median m, the two outer entries sum to 3mu-m.
Distinctness applies across the full construction, including separate triples; case splits can be needed to prove the least overall range.

A property proved for adjacent terms need not hold for separated terms.
A two-term recurrence needs a repeated ordered pair to restart the process; repeating parity states need not mean repeating numerical values.
Prove that an interval bound survives the next update to control distant terms without a closed formula.
Separate a non-repeating start from a later cycle and count from the actual cycle start; periodic sums still require leftover-block checks.

knowledge: A functional counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis everywhere on the required domain or interval.

A nonzero cubic has opposite-sign tails and cannot be positive on the entire real line.

Increasing function height does not imply increasing gradient, and positive height does not imply positive gradient.
An integral of a square is nonnegative, while an ordinary signed integral may cancel.

On a nonempty forward interval, subtract shared integration intervals to isolate a sign constraint; for a continuous function, a nonpositive integral forces at least one nonpositive value, not nonpositivity everywhere.
The distinct roots of a product are the combined roots of its factors, with overlaps counted once.
A nonzero cubic has opposite-sign tails and cannot be positive on the entire real line.

additionalConcepts.title: Draw regions for two-variable inequalities
knowledge: Replace a linear inequality by equality to draw its straight boundary line.
Use a solid boundary for \(\le\) or \(\ge\), and a dashed boundary for strict \(<\) or \(>\).
Test a point away from the boundary to identify the permitted half-plane; inequalities such as \(y>mx+c\) select points above the line.
An AND requires the overlap of the permitted regions, while an OR permits points in either region.
A point on an excluded boundary fails that inequality even if it satisfies every other condition.

example.question: Describe the region satisfying \(x\ge0\), \(y\ge1\) and \(x+y<4\).
steps: Draw solid lines \(x=0\) and \(y=1\), and a dashed line \(y=4-x\).
Keep points to the right of \(x=0\), above \(y=1\), and below \(y=4-x\).
The sloping boundary meets \(y=1\) at \(x=3\), so the allowed horizontal range is \(0\le x<3\).
example.answer: \(0\le x<3\) and \(1\le y<4-x\); the point \((0,1)\) is included and the sloping edge is excluded.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: For simultaneous inequalities, retain the overlap of all regions, not everything shaded by any one condition.

additionalConcepts.title: Estimate equation solutions from intersections
knowledge: The solutions of \(f(x)=0\) are the x-coordinates where the graph meets the x-axis.
The solutions of \(f(x)=g(x)\) are the x-coordinates of intersections of \(y=f(x)\) and \(y=g(x)\).
For simultaneous equations, report both coordinates of each intersection, since both equations must hold at the same point.
Read each scale carefully, interpolate between marked values, and give only the accuracy supported by the graph.
Check the whole permitted interval for further intersections; touching a curve also gives a solution.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification · M4.13, M4.15, M4.16, MM8.7

example.question: To solve \(x^2+x-1=0\), a scaled graph of \(y=x^2\) and \(y=1-x\) shows intersections at approximately \((-1.62,2.62)\) and \((0.62,0.38)\). Give the roots to 1 decimal place.
steps: Rearrange the equation as \(x^2=1-x\), so these graph intersections correspond to its solutions.
Read their x-coordinates: approximately \(-1.62\) and \(0.62\).
Round each x-coordinate to one decimal place.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: An equation in x asks for intersection x-coordinates; do not substitute the intersection heights as the roots.

additionalConcepts.title: Give each allowed input exactly one output
knowledge: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain; different inputs may share the same output.
A one-to-one function has different outputs for different inputs, while a many-to-one function repeats at least one output.
A graph represents a function of x only if each vertical line meets it at most once, with every allowed input assigned a value.
The notation \(\sqrt{x}\) means the nonnegative square root: \(\sqrt9=3\), although solving \(u^2=9\) gives \(u=\pm3\).
The modulus \(|x|\) is distance from zero, so it equals \(x\) for \(x\ge0\) and \(-x\) for \(x<0\); in particular \(\sqrt{x^2}=|x|\).

example.question: Does \(y^2=x\) define y as a function of x on \(x\ge0\)? What changes for \(y=\sqrt{x}\)?
steps: At \(x=4\), the relation \(y^2=x\) allows both \(y=2\) and \(y=-2\).
One allowed input has two outputs, so this relation does not define a function of x.
The rule \(y=\sqrt{x}\) selects only the nonnegative output, giving exactly one output for each \(x\ge0\).
example.answer: \(y^2=x\) is not a function of x on this domain; \(y=\sqrt{x}\) is.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Many inputs giving one output is allowed; one input giving several outputs is not a function.

additionalConcepts.title: Label the sides before using right-triangle ratios
knowledge: In a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle; opposite and adjacent are named relative to the chosen acute angle \(\theta\), with adjacent excluding the hypotenuse.
The ratios are \(\sin\theta=\text{opposite}/\text{hypotenuse}\), \(\cos\theta=\text{adjacent}/\text{hypotenuse}\), and \(\tan\theta=\text{opposite}/\text{adjacent}\).
Pythagoras gives \(a^2+b^2=c^2\) when \(c\) is the hypotenuse; rearrange a ratio to find a length or identify an angle from its known exact ratio.
For a general triangle, a perpendicular height can create right triangles; in three dimensions, select the correct face, cross-section or projection before applying the same rules.

example.question: A right-angled triangle has sides of length \(6\), \(8\) and \(10\), with \(\theta\) opposite the side of length \(6\); find \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\).
steps: The hypotenuse is \(10\), and \(6^2+8^2=10^2\) confirms the right triangle.
Relative to \(\theta\), the opposite side is \(6\) and the adjacent side is \(8\).
Therefore \(\sin\theta=6/10\), \(\cos\theta=8/10\), and \(\tan\theta=6/8\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Opposite and adjacent swap when you change the chosen acute angle; the hypotenuse never changes.

additionalConcepts.title: Solve two equations together
knowledge: A solution of simultaneous equations must satisfy both equations for the same values of the unknowns.
For two linear equations, multiply and add or subtract them to eliminate one variable, or rearrange one equation and substitute into the other.
For a line and a quadratic curve, isolate one variable using the line, then substitute that entire expression into the curve equation.
Solve the resulting quadratic, keeping every allowed root. Substitute each root into the line to recover its paired coordinate.
Check every pair in both original equations. A line and a quadratic curve may have two, one or no real intersections.

example.question: Solve simultaneously \(x+y=5\) and \(y=x^2-1\).
steps: The linear equation gives \(y=5-x\). Both expressions for \(y\) must agree, so \(5-x=x^2-1\).
Rearrange and factor: \(x^2+x-6=(x+3)(x-2)=0\). Hence \(x=-3\) or \(x=2\).
Use \(y=5-x\) separately for each root: \(x=-3\) gives \(y=8\), while \(x=2\) gives \(y=3\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Do not pair the x-value from one root with the y-value from the other. Each intersection is a complete ordered pair.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification: MM1.4 and M4.15, simultaneous equations

additionalConcepts.title: Use all four operations with algebraic fractions
knowledge: Before simplifying, exclude every value that makes an original denominator zero. When dividing by a fraction, also exclude every value that makes the divisor zero.
To add or subtract fractions, use a common denominator. For nonzero denominators, \(\frac{A}{B}\pm\frac{C}{D}=\frac{AD\pm BC}{BD}\); factor first to find a smaller common denominator when possible.
To multiply fractions, multiply numerators and denominators: \(\frac{A}{B}\times\frac{C}{D}=\frac{AC}{BD}\). Factor before cancelling.

To divide by a nonzero fraction, multiply by its reciprocal: \( rac{A}{B}\div rac{C}{D}= rac{AD}{BC}\), with \(B
e0\), \(D
e0\) and \(C
e0\).
Cancel complete common factors, never individual terms across addition or subtraction. Keep original exclusions even when the simplified expression is defined there.

example.question: Let \(A=\frac{2}{x-1}\) and \(B=\frac{1}{x+1}\). Simplify \(A+B\), \(A-B\), \(AB\) and \(A\div B\), stating their domains.
steps: Both original fractions require \(x\ne1\) and \(x\ne-1\). On this domain \(B\) is never zero, so division adds no further exclusion.
For subtraction, retain the numerator bracket: \(A-B=\frac{2(x+1)-(x-1)}{(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{x+3}{x^2-1}\).
Multiply corresponding numerators and denominators: \(AB=\frac{2}{(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{2}{x^2-1}\).
Divide by multiplying by the reciprocal: \(A\div B=\frac{2}{x-1}\times\frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{2(x+1)}{x-1}\). The original exclusion \(x=-1\) still applies.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: When subtracting, subtract the whole adjusted numerator. When dividing, the divisor itself must be nonzero as well as defined.
